events/boniface-fells-oak-723/summary: The English monk Boniface (Wynfrith), commissioned by Rome, cut down the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar in Hesse and used its wood to build a chapel. He organised the German church under papal authority and was martyred in Frisia in 754.
events/iconoclasm-begins-726/summary: Emperor Leo III is traditionally said to have removed the icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate around 726–730, beginning a century of imperial campaigns against religious images. John of Damascus, living under Muslim rule, wrote the classic defence of icons based on the incarnation.
events/iconoclasm-begins-726/causes/0: Military disasters interpreted as divine judgement
events/iconoclasm-begins-726/causes/2: Islamic and Jewish critique of images
events/iconoclasm-begins-726/consequence: Destruction of images and persecution of monks
events/timothy-i-catholicos-780/title: Timothy I, catholicos of the Church of the East
events/timothy-i-catholicos-780/summary: From the new Abbasid capital Baghdad, Catholicos Timothy I led a church spanning from Syria to China. He recorded a courteous debate on Christianity with Caliph al-Mahdi (c. 782), sent missionaries to the Turks and Tibet and appointed metropolitans for India and China.
events/timothy-i-catholicos-780/causes/0: Abbasid patronage of Christian scholars and physicians
events/timothy-i-catholicos-780/conseque: Peak geographic extent of the Church of the East
events/xian-stele-erected-781/summary: The monk Jingjing (Adam) composed a Chinese inscription, with Syriac names of clergy, commemorating 146 years of the 'Luminous Religion' (Jingjiao) in China. Rediscovered around 1625, the stele became the chief proof of early Christianity in China.
events/xian-stele-erected-781/causes/0: Church of the East presence under the Tang
events/xian-stele-erected-781/consequenc: Key primary source for Asian Christianity
events/second-council-of-nicaea-787/summ: Convened by Empress Irene, the Seventh Ecumenical Council restored the veneration of icons, distinguishing honour-veneration (proskynesis) from worship (latreia) due to God alone. 'The honour paid to the image passes to its prototype.' The Frankish court, working from a poor translation, rejected it in the Libri Carolini.
events/second-council-of-nicaea-787/long: After sixty years of imperial iconoclasm, Irene, regent for her son Constantine VI, prepared a council with Patriarch Tarasios and papal legates; an initial attempt in Constantinople in 786 was broken up by iconoclast soldiers. At Nicaea in 787 the bishops grounded icon veneration in the incarnation: because the invisible God became visible in Christ, Christ may be depicted, and the saints and the Theotokos honoured in images. The council's distinction between veneration and worship drew on John of Damascus. A second iconoclast period (815–843) followed, ended by the 'Triumph of Orthodoxy' in 843, still celebrated on the first Sunday of Lent. In the West, Charlemagne's theologians criticised the council, though Rome accepted it. Protestant traditions vary: Lutherans and Anglicans often retain images while rejecting their veneration; Reformed churches have generally seen the council as endorsing idolatry, while Orthodox regard it as defending the reality of the incarnation.
events/second-council-of-nicaea-787/cons: Seventh and last council recognised by Eastern Orthodox
events/coronation-of-charlemagne-800/sum: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's, Rome. The act created a Western Christian empire rivalling Byzantium, tied papacy and Frankish monarchy together and fed centuries of debate over the relation of spiritual and temporal power.
events/coronation-of-charlemagne-800/cau: Papal need for protection against Lombards and Roman factions
Irene ruling in Constantinople as a woman
events/council-of-aachen-filioque-809/ti: Council of Aachen endorses the Filioque
events/council-of-aachen-filioque-809/su: After Frankish monks in Jerusalem were accused of heresy for singing 'and the Son' in the creed, Charlemagne's council at Aachen defended the Filioque. Pope Leo III agreed with the doctrine but refused to add it to the creed, displaying the text without it on silver shields in St Peter's.
events/ansgar-mission-to-scandinavia-829: The Frankish monk Ansgar preached at the Swedish trading town of Birka and later became archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen. His mission had little lasting success, but earned him the title 'Apostle of the North'; Scandinavia was largely Christianised between the late tenth and twelfth centuries.
Archdiocese of Hamburg-Bremen as base for Nordic missions
events/triumph-of-orthodoxy-843/summary: Empress Theodora, regent for Michael III, ended the second period of iconoclasm and restored icons on the first Sunday of Lent 843. The feast of the Triumph of Orthodoxy is still kept annually with a procession of icons.
events/triumph-of-orthodoxy-843/causes/0: Death of the iconoclast emperor Theophilos
events/huichang-persecution-845/title: Huichang persecution of foreign religions in China
events/huichang-persecution-845/summary: Tang Emperor Wuzong suppressed Buddhism and with it the foreign religions, including Church of the East Christianity, ordering monks and nuns to return to lay life. Christianity largely disappeared from China proper until the Mongol era.
events/huichang-persecution-845/causes/0: Economic and nativist reaction against Buddhist monasteries
events/huichang-persecution-845/conseque: Collapse of the first Chinese church
events/gottschalk-condemned-849/summary: The Saxon monk Gottschalk of Orbais taught a strict double predestination drawn from Augustine. Archbishop Hincmar had him flogged and imprisoned; Eriugena wrote against him, but other theologians defended aspects of his view, making this the first great Western predestination controversy.
events/gottschalk-condemned-849/conseque: Debate rehearsed in the Reformation and later Calvinism
events/photian-schism-863/summary: Pope Nicholas I refused to recognise Photius, who had replaced the deposed patriarch Ignatius, and the two sees also clashed over the mission to Bulgaria. In 867 Photius denounced the Filioque and Frankish missionaries' practices; the breach was later healed, but it rehearsed the issues of 1054.
events/photian-schism-863/consequences/0: Filioque becomes a defining Orthodox objection
events/mission-of-cyril-and-methodius-86: Mission of Cyril and Methodius to Moravia

At Prince Rastislav's request, Emperor Michael III sent the Thessalonian brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius to Great Moravia. They created the Glagolitic alphabet and translated Scripture and liturgy into Slavonic, defending vernacular worship before the pope against Frankish clergy.
Rastislav's desire for clergy independent of the Franks
Cyrillic script developed by their disciples in Bulgaria
events/baptism-of-bulgaria-864/title: Baptism of Boris I of Bulgaria
events/baptism-of-bulgaria-864/summary: Khan Boris I accepted baptism from Byzantine clergy, then courted Rome before settling with Constantinople in 870. Disciples of Methodius expelled from Moravia found refuge in Bulgaria, where the Ohrid and Preslav schools produced Slavonic literature and the Cyrillic alphabet.
events/baptism-of-bulgaria-864/consequen: Slavonic literature transmitted to Serbia and Rus'
events/founding-of-cluny-910/summary: Duke William of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny, freeing it from lay and episcopal control under direct papal protection. Cluny's network of priories led a monastic reform stressing elaborate liturgy and helped inspire the Gregorian reform.
events/founding-of-cluny-910/consequence: Model of exemption under papal authority
events/great-lavra-athos-963/title: Great Lavra founded on Mount Athos
events/great-lavra-athos-963/summary: Athanasius the Athonite, with support from Emperor Nikephoros Phokas, founded the Great Lavra, the first large cenobitic monastery on the Holy Mountain. Athos became the spiritual heart of Orthodoxy, drawing Greek, Slav, Georgian and Romanian monks.
events/great-lavra-athos-963/causes/0: Growth of hermit communities on Athos
events/baptism-of-poland-966/title: Baptism of Mieszko I of Poland
events/baptism-of-poland-966/summary: Duke Mieszko I accepted Latin Christianity, partly through his Czech Christian wife Dobrawa, aligning Poland with Rome rather than with the German empire. Gniezno became Poland's archbishopric in 1000.
events/baptism-of-poland-966/causes/1: Need for recognition among Christian rulers
events/symeon-new-theologian-980/title: Symeon the New Theologian at St Mamas
events/symeon-new-theologian-980/summary: As abbot of St Mamas in Constantinople, Symeon taught that every Christian may consciously experience the uncreated light of God, describing his own visions in hymns. His insistence on experiential holiness provoked conflict with church authorities and anticipated hesychasm.
events/symeon-new-theologian-980/causes/: Symeon's own mystical experiences under his elder Symeon the Studite
events/symeon-new-theologian-980/consequ: Influence on hesychasm and the Philokalia
events/baptism-of-rus-988/summary: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kyiv, after marrying the Byzantine princess Anna, was baptized and had the people of Kyiv baptized in the Dnieper. The Primary Chronicle tells of envoys who, in Hagia Sophia, 'knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth'. Ukrainian, Russian and Belarusian Orthodoxy trace their origins to this event.
events/baptism-of-rus-988/causes/1: Vladimir's search for a unifying religion
events/baptism-of-rus-988/consequences/0: Byzantine Orthodoxy in Eastern Slavic lands
events/baptism-of-rus-988/consequences/2: Later contested legacy between Kyiv and Moscow
events/iceland-adopts-christianity-1000/: To avoid civil war, the Icelandic assembly accepted the lawspeaker Thorgeir's ruling that all should be baptized, while private pagan practices were temporarily tolerated. It is a rare example of a negotiated, legal conversion.
Pressure from Norway's King Olaf Tryggvason
events/kerait-conversion-1007/summary: Bar Hebraeus records that the metropolitan of Merv reported the conversion of a Kerait khan and some 200,000 of his people after a vision, asking how they might fast without grain. Kerait and Naiman Christianity later gave Christian wives and mothers to the Mongol royal house.
events/kerait-conversion-1007/causes/0: Church of the East merchants and monks on the steppe
events/kerait-conversion-1007/consequenc: Christian presence at the Mongol court in the 13th century
events/destruction-of-holy-sepulchre-100: Al-Hakim destroys the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem

The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of the Holy Sepulchre and a wider persecution of Christians and Jews in Egypt and Syria. Though later reversed and the church partly rebuilt by Byzantium, the event fed Western crusading memory.
events/great-schism-1054/summary: On 16 July 1054 the papal legate Cardinal Humbert laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates in turn. Though symbolic rather than final, the episode came to stand for the separation of the Catholic West and Orthodox East.
events/great-schism-1054/longText: The schism was the culmination of centuries of estrangement: language (Latin vs Greek), the Carolingian empire, the Filioque, the use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, clerical celibacy and, above all, the reforming papacy's claim to universal jurisdiction versus the Eastern conception of a pentarchy of patriarchs in conciliar communion. Cerularius had closed Latin churches in Constantinople; Pope Leo IX's legates, led by the combative Humbert, came to negotiate but issued an excommunication that technically lapsed with Leo's death. Contemporaries did not see 1054 as final — communion continued in places for decades — and historians stress that the Crusades, especially the sack of Constantinople in 1204, made the division popular and permanent. Reunion attempts at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) failed. In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lifted the mutual excommunications, and theological dialogue continues. Catholics generally describe the division as a schism rather than a heresy and regard the Orthodox as sister churches with valid sacraments; Orthodox views range from similar openness to the conviction that Rome departed from the faith on the Filioque and papal claims.
events/great-schism-1054/causes/4: Norman conquests in Byzantine southern Italy
